title: Valid Anagram
kidExplanation: Two piles of letter tiles. If you can rearrange pile A to look exactly like pile B, they are anagrams — same letters, same counts, maybe different order.
plainProblem: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s (same characters with the same frequencies).

thinkingSteps.title: Brute force idea
thinkingSteps.body: Sort both strings and compare. Easy to understand.

thinkingSteps.title: Why sorting may be enough
thinkingSteps.body: Sorting is O(n log n). Fine for interviews, but counting can be linear.

thinkingSteps.title: Aha insight
thinkingSteps.body: Anagrams have identical character counts. A hash map (or 26 counters) remembers frequencies.

thinkingSteps.title: Better idea
thinkingSteps.body: Count letters in s, subtract letters in t (or compare two maps). If all counts end at zero, they match.

pattern.name: Hash set / hash map for seen items
pattern.whenToSpot: You need fast lookups of values you already saw.

complexity.timeReason: We scan each string once; map updates are average O(1).
complexity.spaceReason: If we only use lowercase English letters, 26 counters are constant space (or O(k) for alphabet size).

edgeCases: Duplicates and boundary values from the constraints.
commonMistakes: Coding before stating the pattern and complexity.
Off-by-one errors on indices or window edges.
Mutating data structures while iterating carelessly.
interviewTips: Name the pattern: Hash set / hash map for seen items.
State O(n) time and O(1) space at the end.
